items.stem: Rahul, a grade nine student, was closely observing his school garden during recess. He noticed the gardener trimming the top shoots of a bushy hedge to give it a neat shape. Surprisingly, after a few weeks, the hedge grew even bushier with many new branches emerging from the nodes of the remaining stems. Curious about plant growth, Rahul also examined a large, freshly cut tree stump nearby and noticed several concentric wooden rings forming its wide diameter. He recalled a science experiment where cutting the extreme tips of onion roots in a water jar completely stopped their downward growth. QUESTIONS: (a) Based on Rahul’s observation of the onion root experiment, why did the roots stop growing when their tips were cut? (b) Which specific tissue is responsible for the new branches sprouting from the nodes of the trimmed hedge? (c) Identify the tissue responsible for the increase in the girth of the tree trunk that led to the formation of the concentric rings.
items.answer: (a) The roots stopped growing because the apical meristem, which consists of actively dividing cells responsible for increasing the length of the plant, is located at the root tips and was removed when the tips were cut. (b) The intercalary meristem, located at the base of leaves or internodes on stems, is responsible for the growth of new branches after the hedge is trimmed. (c) The lateral meristem is responsible for increasing the diameter or girth of the stem, resulting in the concentric rings seen on the tree stump.

items.stem: During a summer camp, children were taught how to make natural fiber baskets. The instructor handed out dried coconut husks and fresh, green, flexible twigs from a climbing vine. He showed the students how the fresh twigs could easily bend into tight circles without snapping, unlike dry wooden sticks that broke instantly. He then asked them to extract the tough, rigid fibers from the coconut husk to bind the twigs together. He explained to the children that specific internal cellular structures give the living green twigs their flexibility and the dead husk its immense strength. QUESTIONS: (a) Name the tissue present in the coconut husk that makes it tough and rigid. (b) Why are the cells making up the coconut husk tissue considered hard and dead? What chemical is deposited on their walls? (c) Which simple permanent tissue allows the fresh green twigs to bend flexibly without breaking? (d) Differentiate between the tissue that provides flexibility to the twigs and the most common tissue that stores food in plants.
items.answer: (a) Sclerenchyma tissue is present in the coconut husk, providing it with strength and rigidity. (b) The cells are hard and dead because they have extremely thick walls due to the heavy deposition of lignin, a chemical that acts like cement and makes the structure woody and stiff. (c) Collenchyma tissue is responsible for providing flexibility and allowing parts of the plant like stems to bend without breaking. (d) Collenchyma tissue consists of living cells with unevenly thickened corners due to pectin deposition, and its main function is flexible support. Parenchyma tissue consists of loosely packed living cells with thin cell walls, and its primary function is the storage of food and sometimes photosynthesis.

items.stem: A team of agricultural scientists was investigating a mysterious wilting disease affecting a large tomato farm. They observed that the soil had adequate moisture, yet the leaves at the top of the plants were drooping and drying out. Upon carefully slicing the stems of the affected plants under a microscope, they discovered that a fungal infection had entirely blocked the inner tubular structures responsible for upward water movement. Meanwhile, the outer tubular structures, which transport synthesized sugars from the leaves down to the roots, remained completely healthy and unaffected by the fungus. QUESTIONS: (a) Identify the two complex permanent tissues mentioned in the scenario as the inner and outer tubular structures. (b) Why is the tissue responsible for transporting water categorized as a complex permanent tissue? (c) How does the cellular composition of the food-transporting tissue differ from the water-transporting tissue in terms of living and dead cells? (d) Predict what would eventually happen to the roots of the plant if the outer tubular structures were blocked instead of the inner ones.
items.answer: (a) The inner tubular structure is the xylem, and the outer tubular structure is the phloem. (b) Xylem is called a complex permanent tissue because it is made up of more than one type of cell working together as a single unit to transport water and minerals. (c) Xylem is mostly made up of dead cells like tracheids, vessels, and xylem fibres, with only xylem parenchyma being living. In contrast, phloem is mostly made up of living cells like sieve tubes, companion cells, and phloem parenchyma, with only phloem fibres being dead. (d) If the phloem were blocked, the roots would stop receiving the food synthesized by the leaves during photosynthesis. Without nourishment, the root cells would eventually die, leading to the death of the entire plant.

items.stem: On a field trip to a botanical garden, Aisha carefully observed two differently adapted plants. The first was a cactus in the desert section, which had a very thick, waxy coating on its outer green stem and no broad leaves. The second was a water lily floating in a nearby pond, with broad flat leaves resting on the water surface. The guide explained that both plants possess an outermost single layer of cells protecting them, but this layer is uniquely adapted to their specific environments. The guide also pointed out that these outer layers contain tiny pores that facilitate interactions with the atmosphere. QUESTIONS: (a) What is the outermost protective layer of cells on both the cactus and the water lily called? (b) Identify the thick waxy coating on the cactus and explain its primary function in a desert habitat. (c) Name the tiny pores found on the epidermis of leaves. What essential physiological process do they enable besides gaseous exchange? (d) Why would having a very thick waxy coating be disadvantageous for the completely submerged parts of an aquatic plant?
items.answer: (a) The outermost protective layer of cells on the plants is called the epidermis. (b) The thick waxy coating is the cuticle. In a desert habitat, it prevents excessive water loss through evaporation, protecting the plant from drying out. (c) The tiny pores are called stomata. Besides gaseous exchange, they enable transpiration, which is the evaporation of water vapours from the plant body that helps in creating a suction pull for water transportation. (d) A thick waxy coating prevents the diffusion of water and dissolved gases. For an underwater plant, this would block the direct absorption of dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide from the surrounding water, which is necessary for respiration and photosynthesis.
items.concept: Epidermis is the protective plant layer

items.stem: Dr. Mehta was reviewing the blood test report of a patient complaining of severe weakness, extreme fatigue, frequent throat infections, and a recent paper cut that took exceptionally long to stop bleeding. He explained to the patient that a specific fluid tissue connecting different body parts was malfunctioning. The lab report indicated a significantly lower than normal count of the oxygen-carrying red cells, explaining the weakness. Furthermore, there was an unusual spike in the specialized cells responsible for fighting infections, and a severe deficiency in the tiny cell fragments needed to seal injuries. QUESTIONS: (a) Which major category of animal tissues does blood belong to, and what is its fluid matrix called? (b) Identify the specific component of blood responsible for the patient’s paper cut bleeding for an exceptionally long time. (c) Which specific blood cells are causing the unusual spike to fight off the patient’s frequent throat infections? (d) Explain why a low count of the oxygen-carrying red cells leads to severe weakness and fatigue in the patient.
items.answer: (a) Blood belongs to the category of connective tissues, and its fluid matrix is called plasma. (b) The patient has a deficiency in platelets, which are the blood components responsible for blood clotting at the site of an injury. (c) White Blood Cells are spiking in number to collect at the infected areas and fight off the germs causing the throat infections. (d) Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which transports oxygen to all body tissues. A low count means the muscle and organ cells receive less oxygen for energy production, leading to severe weakness and fatigue.

items.stem: During an intense ten-kilometer marathon, athlete Sunita felt her leg muscles burning and aching, eventually forcing her to slow down due to extreme fatigue. She noticed that she could consciously control her running pace by deciding when to move her limbs faster or slower. However, despite the intense physical exertion, she realized that her heart was beating rapidly and continuously without her having to consciously think about it. Most importantly, she marvelled at the fact that her heart muscle never felt the same exhausting fatigue that forced her legs to stop moving. QUESTIONS: (a) Which type of muscular tissue is present in Sunita’s legs that she can consciously control during the run? (b) State two structural differences between the muscle cells in her legs and the muscle cells in her heart. (c) Why is it biologically essential that cardiac muscles possess the property of contracting continuously without fatigue?
items.answer: (a) Skeletal muscle, which produces voluntary movements, is present in Sunita’s legs. (b) Skeletal muscle fibres in the legs are unbranched and multinucleate. In contrast, cardiac muscle fibres in the heart are branched and have a single nucleus. (c) The heart must pump blood continuously to supply oxygen and nutrients to the entire body throughout a person’s life. If cardiac muscles fatigued and stopped contracting like skeletal muscles do, blood circulation would halt, leading to immediate death.
items.concept: Cardiac muscle works tirelessly in heart

items.stem: In a busy cooking class, Chef Rohan was distracted and accidentally grabbed a scorching hot metal pan with his bare hand. In a fraction of a second, even before he consciously registered the pain, he violently jerked his hand away from the stove. Later that evening, he noticed a small fluid-filled blister forming on the outermost layer of his skin where it had touched the hot metal. The clinic doctor told him that his skin’s top layer acts as a vital barrier, while a highly specialized biological wire network running throughout his body was responsible for his lightning-fast reaction to the heat. QUESTIONS: (a) Which tissue forms the outermost layer of Chef Rohan’s skin that got blistered, and how are its cells structurally arranged to provide protection? (b) Identify the highly specialized tissue network that allowed him to receive the heat sensation and instantly transmit the message to pull his hand away. (c) What is the fundamental cellular unit of this communication network called? Name its three main structural parts. (d) Explain briefly how the functions of epithelial tissue and nervous tissue fundamentally differ based on this scenario.
items.answer: (a) Epithelial tissue forms the outermost layer of the skin. Its cells are flat, tightly packed with many layers, and have very little space between them to protect underlying tissues from mechanical injury. (b) The nervous tissue forms the body’s control and coordination network responsible for rapid reactions. (c) The fundamental cell of the nervous tissue is called a neuron. Its three main parts are the cell body, dendrites, and axon. (d) Epithelial tissue acts as a physical barrier for protection against injury, fluid loss, and germs. Nervous tissue, on the other hand, is specialized for receiving sensory stimuli and transmitting electrical messages to coordinate body responses.

items.stem: During a competitive football match, a player collided heavily with an opponent and fell to the ground clutching his right knee in immense pain. At the hospital, an X-ray revealed no fractures in the hard, rigid structures supporting his leg. However, a detailed MRI scan showed a severe tear in the tough, elastic connective bands that securely connect his thigh bone to his shin bone to keep the joint stable. The doctor also noted minor wear and tear on the soft, flexible cushioning present at the ends of his leg bones, which usually absorbs shock when he lands from a jump. QUESTIONS: (a) Identify the hard, rigid connective tissue that supports the leg and showed no fractures in the X-ray. (b) Name the specific elastic connective tissues that were torn, which connect bone to bone at the knee joint. (c) What is the soft, flexible cushioning tissue at the ends of the bones called? (d) If the tough bands connecting his calf muscles to his heel bone were injured instead, which connective tissue would be damaged?
items.answer: (a) Bone is the hard, rigid connective tissue supporting the leg. (b) Ligaments are the connective tissues that were torn; they connect bone to bone and provide stability to the joint. (c) Cartilage is the soft, flexible tissue that provides cushioning at the ends of bones to absorb shock. (d) Tendons would be damaged, as they are the connective tissues responsible for connecting muscles to bones.
items.concept: Tendons and ligaments connect body parts

items.stem: A classical Indian dancer, Meera, was choreographing a complex new performance. She started her routine with a graceful, full-circle rotation of her arms originating from the shoulders. Next, she bent her elbows and knees sharply in a rhythmic pattern, restricting their movement to only one direction. Finally, she incorporated rapid side-to-side head movements, looking left and right while keeping her torso perfectly still. A biology student in the audience was fascinated by the biomechanics, noting how different anatomical junctions in Meera’s skeleton permitted such varied, specific, and beautiful ranges of motion. QUESTIONS: (a) Which specific type of joint allowed Meera to perform a complete forward, backward, and circular rotation of her arms? (b) Identify the type of joint present in Meera’s elbows and knees that allows bending movement primarily in only one direction. (c) Name the joint connecting her skull to her backbone that facilitated her side-to-side head movements like a turning doorknob. (d) The flat bones of Meera’s skull protect her brain but cannot move relative to one another. What type of joint connects them?
items.answer: (a) The ball and socket joint in the shoulder allowed for the complete circular rotation of her arms. (b) The hinge joint is present in the elbows and knees, restricting movement to one direction similar to a door hinge. (c) The pivot joint connects the skull to the backbone, allowing the head to move side to side. (d) Fixed joints connect the flat bones of the skull, preventing movement to keep the delicate brain safe.
items.concept: Joints allow movement but need muscles

items.stem: An agricultural research institute was attempting to mass-produce a rare, disease-resistant variety of carrot. Instead of planting normal seeds, a botanist took a tiny fragment of mature, specialized cells from the phloem of a healthy carrot root. He placed these cells in a sterile liquid medium inside a glass flask containing specific nutrients, sugars, and growth hormones. He ensured the mixture was continuously aerated by stirring. Over several weeks, this single mass of specialized cells dedifferentiated, actively divided, and eventually grew into hundreds of identical miniature carrot plantlets ready to be planted in soil. QUESTIONS: (a) What biological term is used to describe the incredible ability of the mature carrot cells to divide and develop into a completely new, entire plant? (b) In the context of tissue culture, why was it necessary to place the carrot cells in a nutrient medium containing sugars and hormones instead of pure water? (c) According to F.C. Steward’s findings, what is the role of dedifferentiation in this experiment?
items.answer: (a) The term used to describe this ability is totipotency. (b) The nutrient medium provides the essential raw materials (like sugars for energy) and chemical signals (hormones) required to trigger cell division and support the rapid growth of the unspecialized cells into a new plant mass. Pure water lacks these necessary components. (c) Dedifferentiation allows mature, specialized permanent tissue cells (like phloem) to regain the ability to divide. They form an unspecialized mass of dividing cells, which can then redifferentiate to form roots, shoots, and eventually a whole new plant.
